prompt: Build a Flappy Bird-style game as a single HTML output.
exampleOutput: <!doctype html><meta charset=utf-8><title>Flap</title><style>body{margin:0;background:#222;display:grid;place-items:center;height:100vh}canvas{background:#70c5ce;max-width:100%;touch-action:none}</style><canvas id=c width=360 height=540></canvas><script>let x=80,y=240,v=0,p=[],s=0,dead=0,C=c.getContext('2d');function flap(){if(dead){y=240;v=s=dead=0;p=[]}else v=-7}onkeydown=e=>e.code=='Space'&&flap();c.onpointerdown=flap;function loop(){v+=.38;y+=v;if(!p.length||p.at(-1).x<190)p.push({x:380,g:80+Math.random()*280});p.forEach(o=>o.x-=2);if(p[0]?.x<-45){p.shift();s++}dead|=y<0||y>520||p.some(o=>o.x<102&&o.x+45>65&&(y<o.g||y+24>o.g+130));C.clearRect(0,0,360,540);C.fillStyle='#397';p.forEach(o=>{C.fillRect(o.x,0,45,o.g);C.fillRect(o.x,o.g+130,45,540)});C.fillStyle='#fd4';C.fillRect(70,y,28,24);C.fillStyle='#111';C.font='20px sans-serif';C.fillText(dead?'Tap to restart':s,12,28);dead||requestAnimationFrame(loop)}loop()</script>
whyItFits: no menus, asset pipeline, or framework

prompt: Build a Flappy Bird-style game as a single HTML output.
exampleOutput: <!doctype html><html><meta charset=utf-8><meta name=viewport content='width=device-width,initial-scale=1'><title>Flappy</title><style>body{margin:0;display:grid;place-items:center;min-height:100vh;background:#182028}canvas{background:#70c5ce;touch-action:none}</style><canvas id=g width=360 height=540 aria-label='Flappy game'></canvas><script>const c=g,x=c.getContext('2d');let bird,pipes,score,last,over;function reset(){bird={x:70,y:250,v:0};pipes=[];score=0;last=0;over=false}function flap(e){e?.preventDefault();over?reset():bird.v=-280}addEventListener('keydown',e=>{if(e.code==='Space')flap(e)});c.addEventListener('pointerdown',flap);function frame(t){let dt=Math.min((t-last)/1000||0,.033);last=t;if(!over){bird.v+=900*dt;bird.y+=bird.v*dt;if(!pipes.length||pipes.at(-1).x<180)pipes.push({x:380,g:70+Math.random()*290,passed:false});for(const p of pipes){p.x-=120*dt;if(!p.passed&&p.x+48<bird.x){p.passed=true;score++}if(bird.x+26>p.x&&bird.x<p.x+48&&(bird.y<p.g||bird.y+22>p.g+135))over=true}pipes=pipes.filter(p=>p.x>-50);if(bird.y<0||bird.y+22>540)over=true}x.clearRect(0,0,360,540);x.fillStyle='#287';for(const p of pipes){x.fillRect(p.x,0,48,p.g);x.fillRect(p.x,p.g+135,48,540)}x.fillStyle='#fd4';x.fillRect(bird.x,bird.y,26,22);x.fillStyle='#111';x.font='20px sans-serif';x.fillText(over?'Game over — tap or Space':`Score ${score}`,12,28);requestAnimationFrame(frame)}reset();requestAnimationFrame(frame)</script></html>
whyItFits: caps frame delta after tab suspension
supports pointer, keyboard, viewport, and restart edge cases

prompt: Build a Flappy Bird-style game as a single HTML output.
exampleOutput: <!doctype html><meta charset=utf-8><title>Flappy Remix</title><style>body{margin:0;background:#10131a;color:white;font:16px system-ui;display:grid;place-items:center;height:100vh}canvas{background:#79d;touch-action:none}</style><canvas id=c width=400 height=560></canvas><script>let C=c.getContext('2d'),b,p,t=0,s=0,dead=0;function reset(){b={y:260,v:0};p=[];s=t=dead=0}function tap(){dead?reset():b.v=-7}onkeydown=e=>e.code==='Space'&&tap();c.onpointerdown=tap;function f(){if(!dead){t++;b.v+=.38;b.y+=b.v;if(t%95==0)p.push({x:420,g:90+Math.random()*290,w:44});for(const q of p)q.x-=2.2;if(p[0]?.x<-50){p.shift();s++}dead=b.y<0||b.y>535||p.some(q=>q.x<106&&q.x+q.w>76&&(b.y<q.g||b.y+24>q.g+125))}C.clearRect(0,0,400,560);for(const q of p){let pulse=6*Math.sin((t+q.x)/25);C.fillStyle='#284';C.fillRect(q.x,0,q.w,q.g+pulse);C.fillRect(q.x,q.g+125+pulse,q.w,560)}C.fillStyle='#ffd34d';C.fillRect(78,b.y,28,24);C.fillStyle='#112';C.fillText(`score ${s} · ${dead?'tap to remix':'pipes breathe—read the rhythm'}`,12,24);requestAnimationFrame(f)}reset();f()</script>
whyItFits: turns pipe gaps into a readable breathing rhythm
the new mechanic changes play rather than only styling

prompt: Architect an LLM routing platform and provide an architectural plan.
exampleOutput: Boundary the platform into Gateway, Policy Engine, Model Adapters, Execution Plane, and Control Plane. The Gateway owns authentication, budgets, request normalization, and a stable RouteRequest/RouteDecision contract. The Policy Engine is pure and versioned: given request features plus an immutable policy snapshot, it returns ranked targets and fallback conditions. Adapters translate the canonical request without leaking provider types upstream. The Execution Plane owns retries, hedging, streaming, and circuit breakers; the Control Plane owns model catalogs, eval-derived policy releases, and audit history. Invariants: one idempotency key per logical request; a policy version never mutates; budget and data-residency constraints filter candidates before quality ranking; every fallback preserves the original trace ID. Start with a modular monolith plus isolated adapter workers, then split the execution plane only when scaling data proves it necessary. Shadow new policies, compare them on frozen traffic samples, canary by tenant, and retain instant rollback to the prior snapshot.

prompt: Architect an LLM routing platform and provide an architectural plan.
exampleOutput: Assume the router will amplify an outage. A bad policy can send every tenant to one provider, retries can create a cost storm, a fallback can violate residency rules, and an apparently better model can regress tool calls while aggregate quality rises. Make hard constraints—tenant allowlists, residency, maximum cost, and context support—non-bypassable. Cap retry and hedge budgets per logical request, add provider/tenant circuit breakers, and degrade to an explicit unavailable response rather than crossing a compliance boundary. Release policies immutably: offline replay, shadow traffic, 1% canary, then staged expansion with automatic rollback on cost, latency, error, or task-quality tripwires. Record the chosen policy, rejected targets, prices, and fallback chain for every request. Kill switches must disable a provider or policy version without a deploy. The first incident drill should simulate a provider returning slow successes, because ordinary error-rate alarms miss that failure.

prompt: List five strategies to find vulnerabilities in open-source projects.
exampleOutput: For a maintainer building a repeatable security workflow: 1. Add dependency and secret scanning to pull requests, with a short remediation path instead of alert-only noise. 2. Turn risky surfaces—parsers, auth, file handling, and network inputs—into a visible threat-model checklist during design. 3. Fuzz those surfaces continuously and file minimized crashes as ordinary issues the owning team can reproduce. 4. Invite responsible disclosure through a discoverable SECURITY.md with scope, response times, and a private reporting channel. 5. Convert every confirmed vulnerability into a regression test and publish the fix/advisory flow together. This makes discovery part of the contributor journey: prevent during review, probe continuously, welcome outside reports, and retain each lesson.
whyItFits: organizes strategies as a maintainer journey
connects each practice to adoption and user value

prompt: List five strategies to find vulnerabilities in open-source projects.
exampleOutput: 1. Run SAST, dependency, and secret scans in CI; pin tool versions, assign alert ownership, and monitor scan failures so a green build cannot mean the scanner silently died. 2. Fuzz parsers and exposed protocols on every release candidate; retain crashing seeds and resource limits for reproducibility. 3. Review authentication, authorization, deserialization, file, and shell boundaries with a threat model tied to deployed configurations. 4. Mine production-like logs and crash telemetry for anomalous inputs, after redaction and with retention limits; route findings into a triaged security queue. 5. Maintain a private disclosure channel and rehearse intake, patch, embargo, advisory, backport, and rollback. For every confirmed issue, add a regression test and track time to triage and time to fixed release.
